The Israelites' Exhortation to One Another to Seek the Lord.</title> <div sID="gen22461" type="x-p"/> At <reference osisRef="Hos.6.4">Ho 6:4</reference> a new discourse, complaining of them, begins; for <reference osisRef="Hos.6.1-Hos.6.3">Ho 6:1-3</reference> evidently belong to <reference osisRef="Hos.5.15">Ho 5:15</reference>, and form the happy termination of Israel's punishment: primarily, the return from Babylon; ultimately, the return from their present long dispersion. <reference osisRef="Hos.6.8">Ho 6:8</reference> perhaps refers to the murder of Pekahiah; the discourse cannot be later than Pekah's reign, for it was under it that Gilead was carried into captivity (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.29">2Ki 15:29</reference>).<div eID="gen22461" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22462" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12311"/><hi type="bold">1. let us return--</hi>in order that God who has "returned to His place" may return to us (<reference osisRef="Hos.5.15">Ho 5:15</reference>).<div eID="gen22462" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22463" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">torn, and ... heal--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Deut.32.39">De 32:39</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.30.17">Jr 30:17</reference>). They ascribe their punishment not to fortune, or man, but to God, and acknowledge that none (not the Assyrian, as they once vainly thought, <reference osisRef="Hos.5.13">Ho 5:13</reference>) but God can heal their wound. They are at the same time persuaded of the mercy of God, which persuasion is the starting-point of true repentance, and without which men would not seek, but hate and flee from God. Though our wound be severe, it is not past hope of recovery; there is room for grace, and a hope of pardon. He hath smitten us, but not so badly that He cannot heal us (<reference osisRef="Ps.130.4">Psa 130:4</reference>). <div eID="gen22463" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: CHAPTER 6 Ho 6:1-11 . The Israelites' Exhortation to One Another to Seek the Lord. They are at the same time persuaded of the mercy of God, which persuasion is the starting-point of true repentance, and without which men would not seek, but hate and flee from God. Though our wound be severe, it is not past hope of recovery; there is room for grace, and a hope of pardon. He hath smitten us, but not so badly that He cannot heal us ( Psa 130:4 ).

Primarily, in type, Israel's national revival, in a short period ("two or three" being used to denote a few days, <reference osisRef="Isa.17.6">Is 17:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.13.32">Lu 13:32</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.13.33">33</reference>); antitypically the language is so framed as to refer in its full accuracy only to Messiah, the ideal Israel (<reference osisRef="Isa.49.3">Is 49:3</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Matt.2.15">Mt 2:15</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Hos.11.1">Ho 11:1</reference>), raised on the third day (<reference osisRef="John.2.19">Joh 2:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.4">1Co 15:4</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Isa.53.10">Is 53:10</reference>). "He shall prolong His days." Compare the similar use of Israel's political resurrection as the type of the general resurrection of which "Christ is the first-fruits" (<reference osisRef="Isa.26.19">Is 26:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.37.1-Ezek.37.14">Eze 37:1-14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.12.2">Da 12:2</reference>).<div eID="gen22464" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22465" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">live in his sight--</hi>enjoy His favour and the light of His countenance shining on us, as of old; in contrast to <reference osisRef="Hos.5.6">Ho 5:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.5.15">15</reference>, "Withdrawn Himself from them." <div eID="gen22465" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12313"/><div sID="gen22466" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12313"/><hi type="bold">3. know, if we follow on to know the Lord--</hi>The result of His recovered favor (<reference osisRef="Hos.6.2">Ho 6:2</reference>) will be onward growth in saving knowledge of God, as the result of perseverance in following after Him (<reference osisRef="Ps.63.8">Psa 63:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.54.13">Is 54:13</reference>). "Then" implies the consequence of the revival in <reference osisRef="Hos.6.2">Ho 6:2</reference>. The "if" is not so much conditional, as expressive of the means which God's grace will sanctify to the full enlightenment of Israel in the knowledge of Him. As want of "knowledge of God" has been the source of all evils (<reference osisRef="Hos.4.1">Ho 4:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.5.4">5:4</reference>), so the knowledge of Him will bring with it all blessings; yea, it is "life" (<reference osisRef="John.17.3">Joh 17:3</reference>). This knowledge is practice, not mere theory (<reference osisRef="Jer.22.15">Jr 22:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.22.16">16</reference>). Theology is life, not science; realities, not words. This onward progress is illustrated by the light of "morning" increasing more and more "unto the perfect day" (<reference osisRef="Prov.4.18">Pr 4:18</reference>).<div eID="gen22466" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22467" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">prepared--</hi>"is sure," literally, "fixed," ordered in His everlasting purposes of love to His covenant-people. Compare "prepared of God" (<reference osisRef="Gen.41.32">Ge 41:32</reference>, Margin; <reference osisRef="Rev.12.6">Re 12:6</reference>). Jehovah shall surely come to the relief of His people after their dark night of calamity.<div eID="gen22467" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22468" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as the morning--</hi>(<reference osisRef="2Sam.23.4">2Sa 23:4</reference>).<div eID="gen22468" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22469" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as the rain ... latter ... former--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Job.29.23">Job 29:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joel.2.23">Joe 2:23</reference>). First, "the rain" generally is mentioned; then the two rains (<reference osisRef="Deut.11.14">De 11:14</reference>) which caused the fertility of Palestine, and the absence of which was accounted the greatest calamity: "the latter rain" which falls in the latter half of February, and during March and April, just before the harvest whence it takes its name, from a root meaning "to gather"; and "the former rain," literally, "the darting rain," from the middle of October to the middle of December. As the rain fertilizes the otherwise barren land, so God's favor will restore Israel long nationally lifeless. <div eID="gen22469" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12314"/><div sID="gen22470" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12314"/><hi type="bold">4. what shall I do unto thee--</hi>to bring thee back to piety. What more could be done that I have not done, both in mercies and chastenings (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.4">Is 5:4</reference>)? At this verse a new discourse begins, resuming the threats (<reference osisRef="Hos.5.14">Ho 5:14</reference>). See opening remarks on this chapter.<div eID="gen22470" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22471" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">goodness--</hi>godliness.<div eID="gen22471" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22472" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">morning cloud--</hi>soon dispersed by the sun (<reference osisRef="Hos.13.3">Ho 13:3</reference>). There is a tacit contrast here to the promise of God's grace to Israel hereafter, in <reference osisRef="Hos.6.3">Ho 6:3</reference>. His going forth is "as the morning," shining more and more unto the perfect day; your goodness is "as a morning cloud," soon vanishing. His coming to His people is "as the (fertilizing) latter and former rains"; your coming to Him "as the early dew goeth away." <div eID="gen22472" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12316"/><div sID="gen22477" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12316"/><hi type="bold">6. mercy--</hi>put for piety in general, of which mercy or charity is a branch.<div eID="gen22477" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22478" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not sacrifice--</hi>that is, "rather than sacrifice." So "not" is merely comparative (<reference osisRef="Exod.16.8">Ex 16:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joel.2.13">Joe 2:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.6.27">Joh 6:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.14">1Ti 2:14</reference>). As God Himself instituted sacrifices, it cannot mean that He desired them not absolutely, but that even in the Old Testament, He valued moral obedience as the only end for which positive ordinances, such as sacrifices, were instituted--as of more importance than a mere external ritual obedience (<reference osisRef="1Sam.15.22">1Sa 15:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.50.8">Psa 50:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.50.9">9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.51.16">51:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.1.11">Is 1:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.12">12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.6.6-Mic.6.8">Mi 6:6-8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.9.13">Mt 9:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.12.7">12:7</reference>).<div eID="gen22478" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22479" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">knowledge of God--</hi>experimental and practical, not merely theoretical (<reference osisRef="Hos.6.3">Ho 6:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.22.16">Jr 22:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.2.3">1Jo 2:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.4">4</reference>). "Mercy" refers to the second table of the law, our duty to our fellow man; "the knowledge of God" to the first table, our duty to God, including inward spiritual worship. The second table is put first, not as superior in dignity, for it is secondary, but in the order of our understanding. <div eID="gen22479" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12317"/><div sID="gen22480" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12317"/><hi type="bold">7. like men--</hi>the common sort of men (<reference osisRef="Ps.82.7">Psa 82:7</reference>). Not as Margin, "like Adam," <reference osisRef="Job.31.33">Job 31:33</reference>. For the expression "covenant" is not found elsewhere applied to Adam's relation to God; though the thing seems implied (<reference osisRef="Rom.5.12-Rom.5.19">Ro 5:12-19</reference>). entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12318"/><div sID="gen22482" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12318"/><hi type="bold">8. Gilead ... city--</hi>probably Ramoth-gilead, metropolis of the hilly region beyond Jordan, south of the Jabbok, known as "Gilead" (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.13">1Ki 4:13</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Gen.31.21-Gen.31.25">Ge 31:21-25</reference>).<div eID="gen22482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22483" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">work iniquity--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Hos.12.11">Ho 12:11</reference>).<div eID="gen22483" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22484" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">polluted with blood--</hi>"marked with blood-traces" [Maurer]. Referring to Gilead's complicity in the regicidal conspiracy of Pekah against Pekahiah (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.25">2Ki 15:25</reference>). See on <reference osisRef="Hos.6.1">Ho 6:1</reference>. Many homicides were there, for there were beyond Jordan more cities of refuge, in proportion to the extent of territory, than on this side of Jordan (<reference osisRef="Num.35.14">Nu 35:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.4.41-Deut.4.43">De 4:41-43</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.20.8">Jos 20:8</reference>). Ramoth-gilead was one. <div eID="gen22484" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 8. Gilead ... city-- probably Ramoth-gilead, metropolis of the hilly region beyond Jordan, south of the Jabbok, known as "Gilead" ( 1Ki 4:13 ; compare Ge 31:21-25 ). work iniquity-- ( Ho 12:11 ). polluted with blood-- "marked with blood-traces" [Maurer]. Referring to Gilead's complicity in the regicidal conspiracy of Pekah against Pekahiah ( 2Ki 15:25 ). See on Ho 6:1 . Many homicides were there, for there were beyond Jordan more cities of refuge, in proportion to the extent of territory, than on this side of Jordan ( Nu 35:14 ; De 4:41-43 ; Jos 20:8 ). Ramoth-gilead was one.

The image is from oxen putting their shoulders together to pull the same yoke [Rivetus]. Maurer translates, "in the way towards Shechem." It was a city of refuge between Ebal and Gerizim; on Mount Ephraim (<reference osisRef="Josh.20.7">Jos 20:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.21.21">21:21</reference>), long the civil capital of Ephraim, as Shiloh was the religious capital; now called Naploos; for a time the residence of Jeroboam (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.12.25">1Ki 12:25</reference>). The priests there became so corrupted that they waylaid and murdered persons fleeing to the asylum for refuge [Henderson]; the sanctity of the place enhanced the guilt of the priests who abused their priestly privileges, and the right of asylum to perpetrate murders themselves, or to screen those committed by others [Maurer].<div eID="gen22486" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22487" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">commit lewdness--</hi>deliberate crime, presumptuous wickedness, from an Arabic root, "to form a deliberate purpose." <div eID="gen22487" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12321"/><div sID="gen22490" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12321"/><hi type="bold">11. an harvest--</hi>namely, of judgments (as in <reference osisRef="Jer.51.33">Jr 51:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joel.3.13">Joe 3:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.14.15">Re 14:15</reference>). Called a "harvest" because it is the fruit of the seed which Judah herself had sown (<reference osisRef="Hos.8.7">Ho 8:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.10.12">10:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.4.8">Job 4:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.22.8">Pr 22:8</reference>). Judah, under Ahaz, lost a hundred twenty thousand "slain in one day (by Israel under Pekah), because they had forsaken the Lord God of their fathers."<div eID="gen22490" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22491" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">when I returned the captivity of my people--</hi>when I, by Oded My prophet, caused two hundred thousand women, sons, and daughters, of Judah to be restored from captivity by Israel (<reference osisRef="2Chr.28.6-2Chr.28.15">2Ch 28:6-15</reference>). This prophecy was delivered under Pekah [Ludovicus De Dieu]. Maurer explains, When Israel shall have been exiled for its sins, and has been subsequently restored by Me, thou, Judah, also shalt be exiled for thine. But as Judah's punishment was not at the time when God restored Israel, Ludovicus De Dieu's explanation must be taken. Grotius translates, "When I shall have returned to make captive (that is, when I shall have again made captive) My people." The first captivity of Israel under Tiglath-pileser was followed by a second under Shalmaneser. Then came the siege of Jerusalem, and the capture of the fenced cities of Judah, by Sennacherib, the forerunner of other attacks, ending in Judah's captivity. But the Hebrew is elsewhere used of restoration, not renewed punishment (<reference osisRef="Deut.30.3">De 30:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.14.7">Psa 14:7</reference>). <chapter eID="Hos.6"/>
